Correlation Measures

Pearson's r: exploring linear relationships

Pearson's correlation coefficient measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two numeric variables.
  • +1: all points lie on an upward-sloping straight line.
  • -1: all points lie on a downward-sloping straight line.
  • Near 0: little linear association, but a nonlinear relationship may remain.
We will explore synthetic data, calculate r step by step, and examine its limitations. No real or confidential data is used. Back to the Notebook Gallery

1. Explore the relationship

Change the slope, noise, and sample size. The random seed stays fixed so changing a control does not create an entirely unrelated random sample. The slope is not the correlation: a shallow, noise-free line still has r = +1 or -1.

2. Calculate r step by step

For paired observations ||((x_i, y_i)||), the sample correlation is ||[ r = \frac{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})} {\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i-\bar{x})^2 \sum_i (y_i-\bar{y})^2}}. ||]Subtracting the means gives deviations. When both deviations have the same sign, their product is positive; opposite signs give a negative product. The denominator scales the result into the interval [-1, 1]. This is also sample covariance divided by the two sample standard deviations. Here is a small example you can calculate by hand:

data.text/html: Both means are 3. The deviation products sum to 8, and each column's deviations^2 sum to 10. Therefore, r = 8 / 10 = 0.80.

data.text/markdown:
Is sample r a maximum likelihood estimator?

Yes, under a particular probability model. If the pairs ||((x_i, y_i)||) are independent and identically distributed observations from a bivariate normal distribution, with unknown means, variances, and population correlation ||(\rho||), then for a nondegenerate sample: ||[ \hat{\rho}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = r. ||]The maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) chooses the parameter values that maximize the likelihood of the observed data under that model.
  • Descriptive statistic: r summarizes linear association without requiring normality.
  • MLE: interpreting r this way depends on the assumed probability model.
  • Bias: r is generally not an unbiased estimator of ||(\rho||) in finite samples, even under the bivariate normal model.
Using n or n - 1 consistently as the divisor in the covariance and both variances gives the same correlation: those factors cancel in the ratio. Using n - 1 does not make the resulting correlation estimator unbiased.

3. Zero correlation does not mean no relationship

Compare a straight line with a symmetric U-shaped relationship below. In the second example, ||(y=x^2||) determines y exactly, yet its sample Pearson correlation is zero (up to floating-point rounding). The rising and falling parts cancel in the correlation calculation. Always inspect a scatter plot alongside r.

4. Interpretation and limitations

  • Use paired numeric observations. Both variables must have nonzero variance. Setting both slope and noise to zero above shows the undefined case.
  • Outliers can change r substantially. A single extreme observation can create or conceal an apparent linear association.
  • Correlation is not causation. Confounding or a shared trend can make two variables correlated without either causing the other.
  • Units do not affect r. Adding a constant or multiplying by a positive constant leaves r unchanged; multiplying one variable by a negative constant reverses its sign.
  • Normality is not required to calculate r. Standard hypothesis tests and confidence intervals need additional assumptions about sampling and distributions. Repeated or time-dependent observations require particular care.
  • Sample r is an estimate. Its population counterpart is called rho (||(\rho||)). Small samples can give unstable estimates; labels such as "strong" or "weak" depend on context.

Try it yourself

  1. Set noise to zero and compare slopes 0.25 and 3. Why is r the same?
  2. Keep a positive slope and increase noise. What happens to r?
  3. Make the slope negative. What changes about the sign of r?
  4. Set the slope to zero with nonzero noise. Why isn't sample r exactly zero?
  5. Explain why the U-shaped example has r near zero despite a perfect deterministic relationship.
